evaluation_context.goal: Produce an excellent, source-faithful learner session while preserving all deterministic correctness, identity, and sequence constraints.
evaluation_context.source_fidelity_goal: Independently verify the hard-gated edited challenger against the supplied source material. Reject unsupported facts, answers, explanations, feedback, or terminology changes; do not edit the artifact.

criteria.factual_fidelity: Every claim and answer is faithful to the supplied source.
criteria.answer_unambiguity: Each item has one defensible answer under its instructions.
criteria.distractor_plausibility: Distractors are credible without becoming defensible answers.

sources.input_id: 8. Get started with generative AI and agents in Azure.md
sources.location: sources/8. Get started with generative AI and agents in Azure.md

evidence.statement: The workplace-use claims and mappings generally match the supplied source: virtual agents support customer inquiries, personalized learning creates tailored quizzes and guides, Copilot supports marketing copy, and coding tools generate snippets, functions, and modules.

The arrange-sentence items allow additional grammatical orders: q4 can form “Generative AI creates custom quizzes based on progress for students,” and q11 can form “Copilot can write product descriptions for marketers from prompts,” so the declared order is not uniquely defensible.
The fill-blank q6 exposes accepted answers as individual strings but declares correct_answer as a serialized array, creating a possible deterministic answer-checking mismatch.
Most distractors are credible neighboring use cases, such as marketing, learning, visual generation, and support, while TPM configuration is a clearly different operational concept.

Distractor rationales explicitly diagnose realistic category confusions such as support versus marketing, learning versus marketing, visuals versus writing, and generation versus deployment configuration.

The foundational definition that generative AI is a subset of artificial intelligence appears at position 6, after five items requiring learners to classify or apply use cases; the sequence therefore introduces examples before establishing the core definition.
The 12-item sequence uses true/false, multi-select, fill-blank, arrange-sentence, and single-choice mechanics, although multi-select and arrange-sentence recur several times.
Prompt stems vary across scenarios and response types, but “Arrange the parts into a correct sentence.” is repeated verbatim three times and “Select all that apply.” recurs four times.
The store-support, education-platform, developer, design-review, and launch-manager scenarios resemble credible workplace decisions tied to the source use cases.
Most incorrect-choice feedback identifies the category error and points to the better-fitting use, but several generic explanations and the q1 intrinsic feedback provide limited next-step guidance.

The session is suitable for a Level 2 identification goal: it combines direct recognition with several workplace-application items, though much of the practice remains straightforward category matching.

Core terms such as virtual agent, personalized learning, image and video generation, product descriptions, and code snippets align across items and with the source; “Copilot” is sometimes shortened from the source’s “Microsoft Copilot.”

The artifact offers broad, source-faithful practice with realistic scenarios and varied mechanics, but answer-order ambiguity, the q6 answer representation, repeated stems, and late placement of the core definition weaken coherence and reliability.

critical_defects.summary: Two arrange-sentence items permit multiple grammatical answers while declaring only one order correct.

evidence.statement: q4 permits both “Generative AI creates custom quizzes for students based on progress” and “Generative AI creates custom quizzes based on progress for students.”
q11 permits both “Copilot can write product descriptions from prompts for marketers” and “Copilot can write product descriptions for marketers from prompts.”

critical_defects.summary: The q6 fill-blank item declares a serialized array as correct_answer instead of one of its accepted answer strings.

evidence.statement: The gap accepts “artificial intelligence” and “AI,” but correct_answer is the literal string “["artificial intelligence","AI"]”, unlike the plain-string correct_answer used by the other fill-blank item.

largest_gap.summary: The session teaches use-case classification before establishing the foundational definition of generative AI.

evidence.statement: The first five ordered items practice customer support, broad uses, natural language, personalized learning, and around-the-clock support; the definition that generative AI is a subset of artificial intelligence does not appear until item 6.

largest_gap.repair_instruction: Move the existing definition item before the use-case classification items, then update sequence paths while preserving item identities and payload content.

result.concise_summary: The session is broadly source-faithful, varied, and appropriate for Level 2, but deterministic answer ambiguity affects two arrange items, q6 has a possible answer-representation mismatch, and the foundational definition is introduced too late. Confidence is reduced because approved_references is empty and reference_confidence_reduced is true.
